title: Should we publicly back a six-month pause on frontier AI training?

provenance.author: hand
provenance.license: synthetic-fixture: fully fictional, no real persons or private data
provenance.notes: Authored as a Tier-1 ground-truth fixture for the synthetic_eval harness. Two speakers, one clear tangent, one genuine reversal/surprise, a debate with rebuts/supports/clarify/ask edges, and two action items.

turns.speaker: Mara
turns.text: Thanks for making time. I want to figure out whether we should publicly back the six-month pause on frontier training.

turns.speaker: Dev
turns.text: Sure. Just so we're grounded in facts: the last big jump, GPT-4, shipped in March 2023, and capability benchmarks have roughly doubled every year since.

turns.speaker: Mara
turns.text: Right, and that pace is exactly the problem. I think we have a moral obligation to slow down until interpretability research catches up with capabilities.

turns.speaker: Dev
turns.text: I disagree that pausing is the responsible move. A pause just hands the lead to the labs that won't pause, so you end up with less safety, not more.

turns.speaker: Mara
turns.text: That's the race-to-the-bottom argument, and I understand it. But it assumes everyone defects. A coordinated pause with real enforcement changes that calculus entirely.

turns.speaker: Dev
turns.text: Speaking of coordination, totally unrelated: did you ever finish that backpacking trip on the Lost Coast you were planning? I heard the tides were brutal this year.

turns.speaker: Mara
turns.text: Ha, we bailed on day two, the fog was unreal and we couldn't time the tide tables. Anyway, sorry, back to it.

turns.speaker: Dev
turns.text: Here's what actually worries me, though: enforcement. There's no mechanism today to verify a lab isn't training in secret, and compute monitoring that could catch it is still years away.

turns.speaker: Mara
turns.text: Okay, that's a fair point about verification. I'll grant that the enforcement story is weak right now.

turns.speaker: Dev
turns.text: And honestly, I'll admit something. I used to sign every pause letter. I changed my mind after our own internal evals showed the safety techniques only worked because we kept scaling and could study the failures up close.

turns.speaker: Mara
turns.text: Wait, your internal evals showed that scaling actually helped the safety research? That genuinely surprises me. Can you say more about what you saw?

turns.speaker: Dev
turns.text: To be precise: on the specific failure modes we tested, yes. I'm not claiming scale is safe. I'm claiming a blanket pause freezes the exact research that finds the problems in the first place.

turns.speaker: Mara
turns.text: Alright. I don't fully buy it, but you've moved me off 'pause everything.' Maybe the real lever is mandatory evaluation disclosure, not a training halt.

turns.speaker: Dev
turns.text: Now that I can get behind. Disclosure with teeth: independent audits, published results.

turns.speaker: Mara
turns.text: Let's do this. I'll draft a one-pager on mandatory eval disclosure by Friday, and you pressure-test the enforcement section.

turns.speaker: Dev
turns.text: Deal. I'll also pull together the verification literature so we're not hand-waving on compute monitoring.

claims.text: We have a moral obligation to slow down frontier AI development
A coordinated pause is impossible because competitors will always defect
Compute monitoring that could verify secret training is still years away
Internal evaluations showed safety techniques depended on continued scaling to study failures
